items.title: Fees and graduate outcomes by subject at a university
points: The table compares annual fees, starting salaries and employment rates six months after graduation for five subjects at a university.
Medicine is the most expensive subject at 42,000 dollars a year, but it also leads to the highest starting salary, 61,000 dollars, and the highest employment rate, 96 per cent.
Fine Art is the cheapest at 22,000 dollars, yet its graduates earn only 26,000 dollars and just 62 per cent are employed after six months.
In general, higher fees go with better outcomes, although Law is an exception, with a lower employment rate of 84 per cent than Business at 88 per cent.
Overall, the more costly professional subjects appear to offer the strongest return for students.

items.title: Rent, commuting time and green space in five cities
points: The table shows average monthly rent, commuting time and the share of green space in five cities.
City A has the highest rent at 2,100 dollars a month, while City D is the cheapest at 950 dollars and also has the shortest commute, 28 minutes, and the most green space, 38 per cent.
For the first four cities, cheaper rent goes together with shorter commutes and more parkland.
City E is the clear exception: its rent is moderate at 1,400 dollars, but it has the longest commute at 64 minutes and the least green space at only 9 per cent.
Overall, the most expensive city does not necessarily offer the best quality of life.

items.title: Average sleep by age group
points: The table compares how many hours people in five age groups sleep on weeknights and at weekends, against the recommended amount.
On weeknights, every age group sleeps less than recommended, with the 41 to 60 group getting the least at 6.6 hours and the over 60s the most at 7.1 hours.
Teenagers aged 13 to 17 show the biggest difference, sleeping 6.9 hours on weeknights but 8.8 hours at weekends, while their recommended figure is 9 hours.
By contrast, the over 60s are the most consistent, sleeping 7.1 hours on weeknights and 7.3 hours at weekends.
Overall, younger people appear to catch up on lost sleep at weekends, whereas older people keep a steadier routine.

items.title: Annual visitors to five museums, 2019 to 2023
points: The table shows the number of visitors, in thousands, to five museums in a city between 2019 and 2023.
All five museums saw a sharp fall in 2020, with Natural History dropping from 820 thousand to 240 thousand, followed by a steady recovery.
Natural History remained the most popular throughout, reaching 870 thousand in 2023, while Local History was the least visited, with 110 thousand in the same year.

The Science museum recovered fastest, passing its 2019 figure of 540 thousand as early as 2022 and reaching 720 thousand in 2023, whereas the Maritime museum, at 190 thousand, was still below its 2019 level of 210 thousand.
Overall, visitor numbers bounced back strongly, although not every museum recovered completely.

items.title: Average broadband speeds in five countries
points: The table shows average broadband speeds, in megabits per second, in five countries from 2016 to 2025.
Speeds rose in every country, and by 2025 Country A was the fastest at 210 megabits per second, while Country E was the slowest at only 34.
The most dramatic growth was in Country D, where speeds climbed from just 9 to 150, more than sixteen times the original figure.
Country C is the notable exception: it led in 2016 at 30 megabits per second but grew slowly to 78, falling to fourth place by 2025.
Overall, the gap between the fastest and slowest countries widened considerably over the period.

items.title: Food consumption per person in three countries
points: The table compares how many kilograms of six types of food each person eats per year in three countries.
Vegetables are the most consumed food in all three countries, with the highest figure of all in Country B at 140 kilograms.
The staple grain differs sharply: Country A eats 95 kilograms of wheat but only 12 of rice, while Country B eats 85 kilograms of rice and only 30 of wheat.
Country A also eats the most meat at 82 kilograms, more than three times the 25 kilograms eaten in Country B, which in turn eats the most fish at 36 kilograms.
Overall, Country C sits between the other two on most foods, suggesting a more mixed diet.

items.title: Participation in sport and exercise by age group
points: The table shows the percentage of people in four age groups who regularly take part in six sports and activities.
Among 16 to 24 year olds the gym is the most popular activity at 38 per cent, while for the over 65s walking dominates at 48 per cent.
Walking is the only activity that rises with age, from 22 per cent in the youngest group to 48 per cent in the oldest.
Football shows the steepest decline, falling from 26 per cent to just 1 per cent, whereas swimming is the most stable, staying between 14 and 21 per cent.
Overall, people move from high-intensity sports to gentler activities as they grow older.

items.title: Energy use per person in five countries
points: The table compares energy use per person, the share of energy from renewable sources and the change in use since 2015 in five countries.
Country E uses the most energy at 55 megawatt hours per person and has the lowest renewable share at just 9 per cent.
Country D uses by far the least, 8 megawatt hours, but its consumption has risen the fastest, by 35 per cent since 2015.
Country C has the highest renewable share at 62 per cent, while Country B has achieved the largest reduction in use, a fall of 12 per cent.
Overall, the heaviest users tend to rely least on renewables, and only two countries have cut their consumption.

items.title: Average monthly student spending by year of study
points: The table shows how much students at a university spend each month on five categories in each year of their degree.
Rent is by far the largest expense and rises every year, from 520 dollars in the first year to 640 dollars in the third.
Spending on books moves in the opposite direction, falling from 110 dollars to only 45 dollars, the lowest figure in the table.
Transport also increases, from 60 to 90 dollars, while social spending drops from 130 to 80 dollars and food stays roughly stable at around 240 dollars.
Overall, housing and travel take a growing share of the budget as students progress, while spending on books and socialising falls.

items.title: Daily household water use by household size
points: The table shows how many litres of water households of one, two and four people use each day for five purposes.
Showering is the largest use in every household, rising from 55 litres for one person to 170 litres for four people.
Kitchen use is the smallest in most cases, at 15 litres for one person and 50 litres for four people.
Garden use is the clear exception, staying almost flat at between 30 and 35 litres whatever the size of the household.
Overall, total use rises from 155 litres for one person to 440 litres for four, so larger households use less water per person.
